name: Bentonite / clay mask

lead: A bentonite mask is a wash-off paste made from an absorbent volcanic-ash clay. It is used in skincare routines for oily or congested skin.
The clay is a well-characterised industrial material, but no clinical studies of its cosmetic effect were found.

paras: Bentonite particles are flat with a large surface area and swell in water, so they adsorb liquids and oils. Proponents attribute the mask's oil-absorbing effect to these properties; any effect is expected to last only until sebum returns.

Bentonite is described as meeting FDA standards for contact with food and drugs, though the FDA has warned about at least one retail bentonite clay product. Individual products and skin reactions vary.

lead: A bentonite clay mask is a wash-off facial or body product whose main ingredient is bentonite, an absorbent clay composed mostly of the mineral montmorillonite. Such masks are marketed for soaking up skin oil and are used in skincare routines aimed at oily or congested skin [1].

Bentonite itself is an industrial and commercial material with many non-cosmetic uses, including drilling fluids, cat litter and wine clarification [1]. No published human trial identified for this article has tested clay masks for oil control or acne, so claims about their cosmetic effects rest on the clay's known physical properties and on user reports rather than on clinical evidence.

Cosmetic product; not a cleared medical device

paras: Bentonite is an absorbent, swelling clay formed largely by the weathering of volcanic ash. The two main commercial types are sodium bentonite, which swells more, and calcium bentonite, which is more common [1].

Its particles are flat and microscopic, giving a large surface area, and it can take up several times its dry weight in water. These properties underlie its use as an absorbent, binder and carrier [1].

In skincare, bentonite is typically mixed into a paste, applied to the face for a period, and rinsed off. Manufacturers and users describe the intended effect as drawing out oil and leaving a matte finish. Medicinal and dermatologic uses of bentonite are historical: it has served as a bulk laxative and as a base for dermatologic formulations [1].

Bentonite is described as meeting US FDA standards for contact with food and drugs, though the same source notes an FDA warning concerning a particular retail bentonite clay product, indicating that individual consumer products can carry risks [1].
